name: Honey (topical)

lead: Topical honey is used as a mask or skincare ingredient for hydration and a softer, brighter look. It is hygroscopic, so it attracts and holds water at the skin surface, and it has a long folk history on burns and wounds.

Its antibacterial properties are attributed to compounds such as methylglyoxal and hydrogen peroxide, under preliminary study. Trials exist for wounds, mouth ulcers and eye conditions, and medical-grade honey products are FDA-approved for minor wounds and burns; trials on cosmetic brightening were not found.

paras: People apply it as a thin layer for a short wash-off mask, mix it with ingredients such as oats or yoghurt, or use it as an ingredient in cleansers and creams. Hydration shows right after rinsing.
Generally well tolerated as a food. Infant botulism is the best-documented risk of honey, so it is not given to infants under one, and allergy is possible in sensitive people.

angle.text: Honey draws moisture into the skin surface, so it is used in masks and skincare for softer, hydrated, glowier-looking skin, and some people use it for brightening and blemishes. Its documented research is in wound care.

lead: Topical honey refers to honey applied to the skin, either as a home remedy and mask ingredient or as a processed ingredient in skincare. Honey is hygroscopic, meaning it draws in moisture, which is the basis for its use as a humectant [1]. It also has a long folk use on burns and skin injuries [1].

In appearance skincare, honey is promoted for hydration, softening and a 'brightening' or clarifying effect. Clinical research on honey has focused mainly on wound care and mucosal conditions rather than on cosmetic skin outcomes.
Wikipedia reports that medical-grade honey products have been approved by the FDA for minor wounds and burns, while evidence for many other uses is low quality [1].
infobox: Not recommended for infants under one (botulism) [1]

paras: Honey appears in DIY face masks and in commercial moisturisers, cleansers and masks, usually for hydration and softening. Traditional-brightener claims exist in beauty literature, but none of the sources reviewed provide controlled data on skin tone or pigmentation.

Honey has long been used as a topical antibacterial in traditional medicine, and its antibacterial effects were first reported in 1892; potency differs widely between honeys [1]. Wikipedia describes preliminary evidence that honey heals partial-thickness burns several days faster than other dressings and moderate evidence for faster healing of post-operative infections, with low-quality evidence for other wound uses [1]. Clinical reviews list honey among topical options for MRSA and chronic wounds [2][3].

Human trials of honey are largely in wound and oral settings. A randomized, blinded trial compared honey with a topical corticosteroid for recurrent minor aphthous ulcers [4]. A randomized assessor-masked trial of 16% manuka honey eye-drops studied meibomian gland dysfunction [5]. Registered trials include honey dressings versus EUSOL for wound infection, honey in deep neck abscess care, manuka honey after third-molar surgery, diabetic foot ulcers, perineal tear healing and honey versus alcohol as a skin disinfectant [6][7][8][9][10].
No controlled human study of honey for facial brightening, wrinkles or skin hydration was identified among the sources reviewed.

Honey is generally considered safe in typical food amounts, but infants under one year can develop botulism from honey containing Clostridium botulinum spores [1]. Wikipedia also notes possible interactions with allergies and that people with weakened immune systems may face infection risk [1]. Topical allergic reactions in sensitive individuals are possible, though the reviewed sources do not quantify them.

timeline.event: Antibacterial effects of honey first reported [1].
